opus-5.5.text:
I've always thought of autonomous driving as the first large-scale deployment of embodied AI. If you look at it technically, a self-driving car is a robot: it has to perceive the environment, understand what's happening, make decisions, and then act in the physical world, all in real time and with very high safety requirements. That perception, cognition, decision, and action loop is exactly the same loop a robot has to close.

So the technology stack overlaps heavily. On perception, it's sensor fusion: cameras, lidar, radar, and building a 3D understanding of the world. On the cognitive side, it's prediction, planning, and increasingly end-to-end models that go from pixels to actions. And underneath all of that is the data loop: collecting data, simulation, generating long-tail scenarios, training, and redeploying. Much of what the autonomous driving industry built over the past decade, the simulation platforms, the data infrastructure, world models, is directly transferable to robotics.

But there are important differences. A car operates in a relatively structured environment. There are roads, lanes, traffic rules, and the action space is basically steering, acceleration, and braking. A general-purpose robot, especially a humanoid, faces a much more open environment and a much more complex action space. It has to grasp, manipulate, and interact with objects and people. Dexterous manipulation is a much harder problem, and we don't yet have the equivalent of millions of cars on the road generating data every day. Data scarcity is probably the biggest bottleneck for robotics right now.

So my view is that autonomous driving is a precursor and a training ground. It's where we learned how to bring AI out of the digital world into the physical world safely and at scale. Robotics is the next, broader frontier. The convergence point is foundation models for the physical world, vision-language-action models and world models that can generalize across different bodies, whether that body is a car, a drone, or a humanoid.

I often say information intelligence was the first wave, physical intelligence is the second wave, and eventually biological intelligence, AI connected with the human body and the brain, is the third. Autonomous driving is the leading edge of physical intelligence, and robotics will carry it much further.

r001.rationale: The response describes general-purpose robots as facing more open environments and more complex action spaces, and calls dexterous manipulation much harder than driving.

r002.rationale: It mentions autonomous driving’s high safety requirements but does not say it requires greater precision than robotics generally does.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says autonomous driving and robotics share the perception, cognition, decision, and action loop.

fable-5.1.text:
I've always said that autonomous driving is really the first large-scale robot. If you think about what a robot needs, it needs perception, decision-making, and control. It needs to understand the physical world, and then it needs to act in it. An autonomous vehicle does exactly that. It's a robot on four wheels operating in an open, unstructured environment, with very high requirements for safety and reliability.

So technically the two are deeply connected. Many of the capabilities we built up over the past decade in autonomous driving carry over almost directly. Multi-sensor fusion, mapping and localization, prediction of other agents' behavior, planning under uncertainty, and increasingly end-to-end learning from large amounts of data. The robotics community is now facing the same questions we faced in driving: how much do you rely on rules and modules, and how much do you let the model learn from data?

But there are also important differences. Driving is actually a relatively constrained task. The vehicle moves in a two-dimensional space, the rules of the road are well defined, and the action space is small. Steering, throttle, brake. A general-purpose robot, especially a humanoid, has to manipulate objects, which is much harder. High degrees of freedom, contact-rich interaction, and an enormous diversity of tasks and environments. Perception is also harder, because you need fine-grained understanding of objects, not just drivable space and obstacles.

The other big difference is data. In autonomous driving we were fortunate. Millions of cars on the road generate massive amounts of real-world data, and the cost of collecting it is low. Robotics does not yet have that flywheel. That's why people are working so hard on simulation, on teleoperation, on learning from video, and on foundation models that transfer knowledge across embodiments.

So my view is that autonomous driving is a special case of embodied intelligence, and in many ways it was the pathfinder. The talent, the tooling, and the engineering discipline we built there are now flowing into robotics. At the same time, the breakthroughs in large models are giving robots a kind of common sense and generalization ability that we never had in the driving era. I think the two fields will converge, and in the next several years we will see them increasingly share the same underlying models and infrastructure.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts constrained driving with general-purpose robotics, describing robot manipulation as much harder and involving more degrees of freedom and task diversity.

r002.rationale: It says autonomous driving has high safety and reliability requirements, but does not state that it requires greater precision than robotics generally does.

r003.rationale: It says both require perception, decision-making, and control: understanding the physical world and acting in it.

astra-6.text:
I see autonomous driving as a form of robotics. A self-driving car is a robot that perceives its surroundings, predicts what might happen, plans its actions, and then controls its movement. Those same capabilities are central to robotics more broadly.

The difference is in the environment and the tasks. A car operates mainly on roads, where there are traffic rules, but also considerable uncertainty and very demanding safety requirements. A robot in a home or factory may need to manipulate objects, move through tight spaces, and interact with people in different ways.

So there is a great deal of shared technology—sensing, perception, planning, control, and learning—but you cannot simply transfer the entire system unchanged. I think advances in autonomous driving will help robotics, and advances in robotics will also feed back into autonomous driving.

r001.rationale: The response compares environments and tasks but does not say robotics is generally more technically complex than autonomous driving.

r002.rationale: It mentions autonomous driving’s demanding safety requirements, but does not state that it requires greater precision than robotics generally does.

r003.rationale: It describes both fields as sharing the capabilities of perceiving surroundings, predicting what may happen, planning actions, and controlling movement.

sol-6.1.text:
I see autonomous driving as a form of robotics. The car is a robot operating in an open, dynamic environment: it has to perceive the world, understand what is happening, predict how other participants will move, and then plan and act safely.

Those capabilities are also central to robotics more broadly. Advances in sensors, machine learning, simulation, and planning can benefit both fields. But the challenges differ. A car has a relatively constrained set of actions—steering, accelerating, and braking—while a general-purpose robot may need to grasp objects, manipulate tools, and interact with people in many different settings.

So there is a strong shared technical foundation, but progress in autonomous driving does not automatically solve robotics. It gives us valuable technology and experience, especially in building systems that must work reliably in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response notes that general-purpose robots may handle more varied tasks, but does not state that robotics is generally more technically complex than autonomous driving.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the precision required in autonomous driving with robotics generally.

r003.rationale: It describes both fields as sharing capabilities to perceive, understand, predict, plan, and act, which communicates a shared perception–understanding–action foundation.
